U.S. Workers Admitted Rockport. Unemployed Claim Unfair Treatment Brockville, Ont., April 16.-Considerable feeling has been aroused in the Rockport area, in the Thousand Islands, through immigration officials permitting United States carpenters, painters and other tradesmen^ to enter the country for the purpose of carrying ont renovation and improvements to summer homes in the vicinity owned by Americans while Canadian residents of the neighbourhood remained unemployed.
I also wish to draw attention to another despatch which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of yesterday, the 16th instant, and which carries the information that the United States government, in order to protect the interests of its citizens, is taking steps to deport 30,000 French Canadians from the New England states.
The question which I wish to ask is this: Will the Minister of Labour or the Acting Minister of Labour, when the opportunity presents itself, as it apparently does in this Brockville case, retaliate against the United States government by deporting to their own country those painters, carpenters and other tradesmen who appear to be doing work which should be carried on by Canadian citizens.

The house resumed from Thursday, April 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Max D. Cormier for an address to His Excellency the Administrator in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the house on a resolution which has been debated for something over three weeks one naturally feels that almost everything which could profitably be said has been said. However Canada is a big country and it has many problems. I believe that with the situation now prevailing, economically and socially the most serious which has prevailed for fifty years, it is our duty to explore every phase of the situation as thoroughly as possible in an effort to learn the causes and if possible to suggest some solution.
Before proceeding further, Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate you on your almost complete restoration to health and to express the wish which is in the heart and mind of every hon. member in this house that you will be long spared to preside over its deliberations. I also wish to congratulate the mover and seconder of the resolution on the very able manner in which they dealt with the whole question now before us. I wish also to congratulate the government on the scope and character of the speech from the throne the details of which we will have ample opportunity to discuss as the session proceeds. Particularly I wish to congratulate the government on the vision and courage of which it has given evidence in the action it took at the special session of parliament to meet a situation inherited 'by them from their predecessors, the most difficult that any government in Canada has ever been called upon to face. They are to be congratulated equally on the success of the measures taken during that session to meet that emergent situation.
Particularly at this time I wish to refer to the action taken for the relief of unemployment. There is no use side-stepping such a question; there has been and there is serious unemployment in Canada. I state however without fear of satisfactory contradiction that there never has been a time in this country where so complete cooperative and favourable action has been taken between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities, employers of labour, and charitable institutions to meet a critical situation. As a result of the legislation passed at the special session of par-
Lament and the action taken by the Department of Labour under that legislation some 230,000 men have been given employment. True, in many cases the work was not of a character to which many of the men had been accustomed. Men who had been employed as mechanics and railway employees were given employment in road construction, mining and railway construction; nevertheless they got employment. Knowing the situation among many of these men and having been constantly in contact with them I wish to say now that they have nothing but gratitude in their hearts for the measures taken to relieve the situation with which they were face to face.

Now, Mr. Speaker, let me say most emphatically that in my opinion agriculture could not possibly be in a worse condition than it is to-day, and the effect of all this is that every business and professional man in the west is feeling the effects of this depression. The farmer finds it absolutely impossible to pay his debts. For many years a practice has prevailed in rural centres whereby the local storekeeper has grubstaked the farmer and every fall the farmer has come in and paid his account. To-day he cannot do so and consequently the storekeeper has been unable to pay his debts, with the result tha:. he is liable to be closed out by his own creditors, and many of these storekeepers are liable to be made bankrupt. The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) has stated that a large percentage of his constituents are bankrupt. I will go further and say that this would be true of almost all the people in western Canada, in view of the definition of bankruptcy given in section 3 of the Bankruptcy Act. This definition reads as follows "a debtor commits an act of bankruptcy in each of the following cases"-here follows a list of cases all lettered alphabetically, until we come to the last one, which reads:
(j) If lie ceases to meet his liabilities generally as they become due.
Everyone will realize that according to this definition a very large number of people in the prairie provinces could be declared bankrupt. I have a practical suggestion to make to the government, and ask that even though it comes from this side of the house it be given sympathetic consideration. It is that the Bankruptcy Act be amended either by striking out subsection (j) or alternatively suspending its operation during the present period of depression. Many local merchants are being threatened by their creditors that they will be put into bankruptcy unless they make a voluntary assignment. While these men may be bankrupt according to the strict letter of the law, they are not insolvent. I know many men who although they cannot pay their debts as they fall due, yet have a substantial surplus of assets over liabilities. Should they make a voluntary assignment or be forced into bankruptcy, all this surplus disappears. Their stock is sold for about 40 to 50 cents on the dollar and after the trustee's expenses have been paid, the creditor gets little and the debtor is broke.

Our object must be not crass indifference to the interests of all other nationals, not just cold blooded exploitation, but to provide work for all Canadians. We must ever keep before us the improvement in the Canadian standard of living, which our resources, education, and civilization will make a simple task if we have courage, energy and faith. To better our standard of living we must be prosperous, and Canada is not prosperous to-day. The advantage in world commerce, the place in the sun, will belong to that nation which first and best realizes the necessities of the present world economic position.
I am advocating the immediate adoption of a policy that otherwise we shall be forced into in a very short time, and if we wait for that day it is not inconceivable that our present institutions might not be then in control of the working out of that policy. Science, machinery, transportation, communications, are forcing the world forward at an ever increasing rate. The immediate future offers nothing but economic war; civilization demands a truce to regulate production through reducing the hours of work; civilization demands a world economic peace. In this new' world away from the age-old distrusts of the old world, let all the nations assemble to cooperate for the benefit of mankind. A suggestion I wish to make to the Prime Minister is that there is no other place in the world to-day where the question of international economic cooperation can be so well considered as it can be right here in Canada. Until that day, when world economic peace has been proclaimed, let us Canadians, with faith and courage, set our course to make Canada the barometer of world trade.

Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house for only a shout time to make a few observations. Since eight o'clock we have had the pleasure of listening to two excellent addresses. This recalls to my mind the words used by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) during his election campaign when he went throughout the west calling upon sinners to repent. It seems to me that those two splendid addresses are calling upon sinners to repent.
I should like in this public way to say how pleased I am at the elevation to a ministerial office of my old school friend and lifelong chum, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland), which has brought so much credit to the good old county of Oxford, half of which each of us represents. I see

The Address-Mr. Cayley
my friend the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) applauding; he too is an offspring of that good old county. With regard to the criticism that has been hurled against the front benchers on the other side for being absent so much, I should like to point out that my good friend from North Oxford, the Minister of National Defence, is not among that class. He has shown a great deal of interest at all times in the affairs of the house.
I want also to pay tribute to another old chum of mine in the person of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), with whom I had the privilege of attending school for some months. He has said that he is faced with a very heavy task, and I am sure he is. I want to assure both of these hon. gentlemen that in any effort which they undertake for the improvement of conditions in Canada, I shall personally be only too happy to cooperate with them, for my love of Canada is no less than theirs.
Listening to the addresses from different members from all parts of Canada, and knowing conditions in his own locality, one must admit that the world is passing -through dark days, and in spite of the attempt on the part of some to claim that conditions in Canada are only a legacy from the King administration, the consensus is that the present situation is due to world economic conditions If the government headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) ever goes out of power-and it is -being prophesied now that this will happen soon-let us hope that his government will not leave any worse legacy than the one they took over. The King administration saved Canada from a much more serious state than would have been the case had they not been in office prior to the accession to power of the party opposite.
In a recent article in the New York Times, Raymond B. Fosdick, a distinguished lawyer and author, describes conditions as follows:
In a world that is bursting with goods and that has limitless capacity to produce, we are haunted by the spectre of compulsory idleness with its bony fingers upon the throat of our industrial life. Apparently the problem of the machine age is not so much a problem of producing goods as it is a problem of producing buyers. The unemployed are waiting for the flow of wages so that they can buy goods they need. The manufacturers with idle plants are waiting for consumers with sufficient money to start the wheels. All unwillingly we have slipped into the vicious circle.
The progress of science and invention has brought the world to this emergency. So must it lead us out into better times of its solution.
Some say we must do away with the machine and go back to more and more hand labour. But we cannot go back. The discoveries of modern times must carry us forever forward. There is no standing still, no going back, but ever the bringing to light of new -forces and ever changing conditions, to which -changing conditions the world must adapt itself.
The Right Hon. J. H. Thomas, Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, -in his statement before the 1930 Imperial conference used these significant words:
I would, therefore, sir, put to the conference this proposition. What we must apply ourselves to is how this conference, representative of the empire as a whole, can make a practical contribution toward the solution of the difficulties and problems we are faced with to-day, but I say a practical proposal and I say practical remedies, because we are faced with circumstances in which quack remedies and mere phrases or preorations will not lead to real results.
A quack is a pretender to medical or other skill, so the dictionary informs me. He usually has the one and only panacea for all ills. Such was the medicine man with his incantations and charms. His treatment may pacify and soothe -for a time, but seldom effects a permanent cure. Industrial success to-day is due to the elimination of the quack remedies in that sphere of activity; but in the world of politics and statecraft, the charmer and medicine man still holds sway. In this connection one may -recall the case of the sick Indian medicine man who was asked why he did not beat the drum for himself and take -his own medicine. His reply was, "Sometime drum all right, sometime medicine all right, but me sick." Canada is sick, but this government continues the use of the old time quack medicines, incantations and charms.
The need for reconstruction on a broad basis is urgently felt, as Mr. Thomas further points out, saying, "It is hardly necessary for me to say that the world has struck an economic blizzard"; and he implored all the representatives to forget "party," and forget "election promises" in the face of the great emergency, and suggest some practical remedy. One realizes now how incriminating those words sound in the face of Canada's un-ipre-ferential legislation of the special session of last autumn, and the bold, blunt proposals of Canada's Prime Minister, in which he outlined his "Canada first" policy.
With here and there a jarring note, one, nevertheless feels that the nations are beginning to realize that our political conceptions have not caught up with our machines and that we still cling to the idea that we
The Address-Mr. Cayley

can maintain, political isolation in a world in which economic isolation has long since gone by the board. This is our challenge.
We have the League of Nations-a world council of justice-great world conferences, material and religious-and we have our Imperial conferences, all in an endeavour to create a wider political system better able to protect the more extensive intersts of the nations they serve.
Higher and higher discriminatory tariffs are quack remedies. There seems to have developed an insatiable greed for tariffs, to build about us an insurmountable wall so that our only recreation will be that of charging each other high prices. Tariffs may be wisely applied, but in order to apply them sanely and wisely a government must have at its disposal all the data it can possibly obtain from a far-reaching investigation. For tariffs may be highly discriminatory, as was found to the dismay of the present government in the case of glass. A tariff board of well-trained impartial experts, non-ipolitical, nonpartisan, is an absolutely necessary adjunct of every government, and it is with great satisfaction that one learns of the government's intention to re-establish the tariff board which they so ruthlessly exterminated on coming into power.
We should learn from the past. Canada has had extraordinary periods of growth and prosperity. In those periods sprang into being her great industrial centres, her great ports and transportation systems. Then were settled, and tilled ever-increasingly, millions of acres of fertile land. Then Canadian shipping was found in the ports of the seven seas. Foreign commerce increasingly sought our shores. Canada flourished because her world trade flourished. Canada's growth in the fifteen years of the Laurier regime was wonderful, but the golden era of her prosperity was during the nine years of the Mackenzie King administration. I might implore this government to forget its pre-election promises, but that is unnecessary, as hon. members have so often pointed out. But I would urge that they formulate their policies along those lines which brought Canada such success during the regimes of these great Canadian statesmen, and welcome the coming Imperial conference in the spirit of the Dunning budget. This parliament might well, too, study the causes of the depression with a view to preventing its repetition; and not merly accept its recurrence as an act of providence but rather as a problem for sober-thinking representatives of a great people to solve. I do not doubt for a moment the ability of the 
present age to solve the economic problems of such a crisis as the present, when machinery has not only captured the workshop but is invading the home and leaving its impact on social and family- life. The great fact of to-day is the collapse of man power before machinery and narrow governmental policies. The solution will be found in a careful adjustment of conditions both at home and internationally. It will not be found in a wholly free trade policy, or in an exclusive high tariff policy, but in the careful adjustment of a free trade and moderately protective and mutually beneficial policy.
Foreign trade is not war but exchange. When Canada's ambassador to Tokyo seeks to sell wheat to Japan he is asked "what will Canada buy from us"? When he goes to China, China wants to know what Canada will buy from her. When the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald) seeks a market for potatoes in Cuba he will be asked the same question. When the Prime Minister endeavours to sell Canadian wheat in the motherland it is pointed out that the old land buys from Canada many more millions of dollars' worth than Canada buys from her, and the question is asked whether Canada will take more. What will Canada buy from Britain?
At present it would appear that the "Canada first" policy may have the effect of greatly reducing Canadian foreign trade. Already from one cause or another it is greatly reduced. Exports are falling off, our industries are languishing and unemployment becoming more and more a problem. It is true there is no great trek of our youth to the United States, for that country is in a worse economic condition; but a number of Canada's trained workmen and those technically trained are joining the large army going into Russia. Stephen Leacock, Professor of Economies at McGill University, speaking a few days ago under the auspices of the Montreal junior board of trade in the Windsor Hotel, is reported as saying:
Russia is going to fail; Russia is going to break. In Russia there is none of the apparatus of democracy as we know it-nothing but a huge driven herd of millions scarcely worth while counting. But they put Russia together.
The professor does admit that they are doing things in Russia, and it will be all the more difficult for the rest of the world where things languish.
Their political organization is on the pattern of political parties in the United States; their economy is copied from the American trusts.

Further on Mr. Leacock is reported as saying:
Wliat are we going to do ? The virus of communism is eating into the souls ot the young people of Canada because we are not doing enough for the country and they know it; because we starving in a land of plenty and they know it. We must build something here which will be a bulwark against any communistic chance.
Continuing he says:
It is whether Russia will break or we will break first. In Canada we will have to be up and doing. We have the resources-more than 10.000.000 people could live here if they wanted. If Russia can build dams, pile up production, so can we. But we produce too much. Hitherto we thought of that as a kind of interesting paradox. We have to solve it. We must have a policy which will mean that there must be bread and work for all. Not the English dole system-all bread and no work that is no good.
The greatest problem, and the one that comprehends and includes all others, is the improvement of agriculture in Canada. The future of Canada is dependent upon having a prosperous happy and contented rural population. For agriculture is the basic industry. And in view of the urgent demand, arising out of the serious condition in which Canadian farmers find themselves, parliament would do well to spend a greater part of its time during this session in committee trying to find a solution for their difficulties. I am not going to attempt to describe conditions in my own county. Perhaps they are not as bad as they are in some other counties, but meeting farmers continually and knowing them intimately I do say that many of them have made committments and find themselves wondering how they are going to get through. They are a brave class of people. They come from a noble group of people who pioneered this country, and they are not easy to discourage.
I am going to quote from what I believe to be one of the best sources from which we could draw information regarding the condition of agriculture in Canada to-day. I have in my hand a manifesto on agricultural conditions, issued by the Canadian Council of Agriculture. This information is not gleaned from any particular part of Canada, but from Canada as a whole. The council knows whereof it speaks, and issues the following statement:
The conditions now prevailing among the agricultural population of the Dominion menace the whole social and economic fabric of tlie country. Exhortations to optimism and statements denying the widespread suffering and impoverishment of our rural people, even when made by prominent men, do not change the facts. Farmers are being reduced to
poverty; their families are being inadequately fed, clothed and educated; they are unable to meet their obligations to pay taxes, to redeem mortgages, to maintain payments of interest, to settle their debts for machinery, gas and oil, and other necessary purchases. Many lack seed for spring sowing and will be compellea to go deeper into debt in order to provide it. Even the minority who have hitherto occupied a position of financial independence have "gone behind" and are in danger of being submerged.
For many years the Canadian Council of Agriculture, speaking for the farmers provincial organizations, has protested against the handicaps imposed on the farming industry by tariff exactions, high transportation costs, inadequate and expensive credit facilities and inequitable taxation, to name only the more outstanding of their grievances. Such protests have been unavailing and the advent of the world-wide depression, resulting from the costs and ravages of the war, aggravated by the national jealousies and economic rivalries which have succeeded it, has found the Canadian farmers totally unable to cope with the difficulties and to make the sacrifices entailed by it. The continuance of the existing conditions throughout another crop year must inevitably involve in the most serious degree the financial and industrial institutions of the Dominion. Banks, trust companies, mortgage corporations and other lending institutions will find themselves in possession of the lands and chattels which form the security for their loans, but lacking purchasers to take them off their hands. Their security will have depreciated to an extent necessitating the writing off of very heavy losses. The manufacturing concerns, together with the great army of distributing agencies, will face stagnation owing to the inability to find purchasers for the products they produce or handle. The farmers will be either dispossessed or compelled to spend long years in carrying on an uphill struggle to liquidate the debts of principal and interest pyramided upon them. Large numbers will become tenant farmers, or farm labourers, living at a standard much below that, even, which they have been able to attain in the past.
I have heard from both sides of the house different suggestions as to the reason for the unfortunate position in which the farmers find themselves. Some people blame the farmers for laziness; some allege mismanagement; some say they are buying too much and some that they are buying too little. If there is any class of people in the Dominion of Canada which receives from the arm-chair and white-collared philosophers of our land more free advice than any other class, it is the poor farmers. In the present emergency they require some one really to show them how to surmount the difficulties which confront them. Show them what? How to do all the work on a 100-acre farm without help-grow, harvest and market the crops; build the buildings and keep them in repair; be machinist, agriculturist; pay the interest on the mortgages, pay the taxes; feed and clothe his family; support the church and local in-
The Address-Mr. Cayley

stitutions, and the other hundred and one things which time does not permit me to enumerate.
The farmer finds himself confronted with heavy capital commitments at a time of falling prices for his own productions. He is endeavouring to meet the payments of high-priced farms and equipment in the face of an income barely sufficient to maintain the living expenses of his own household. As I said, the betterment of the fanners' condition involves to a large extent the solution of the other great problems of industrial regeneration and unemployment. In view of the positive promises given to the countiy by the Prime Minister, that he would right the wrongs of the Canadian people, the farmers of Canada are awaiting with keen expectation the coming of that great day of fulfilment.
Considerable criticism has been offered by hon. members of Canadian banking institutions. Perhaps they might do more by way of assistance, but when one recalls the wholesale failures of banks in the neighbouring republic and their instability one must feel increased pride and confidence in Canadian banks.
What is most important is the adaptation of our institutions to modern conditions and needs, based on a world-wide conception. Internationally we are interdependent; we cannot live to ourselves; we all need markets and we all need each other. I say to-day is the empire's chance. For this emergency has she been preserved. Her's the chance to consolidate-to solve the great economic and social problems and preserve peace and freedom among 450,000,000 people. There is urgent need for an empire board to be working all the time, not periodically; a board, not of politicians but of experts in their particular lines. I repeat, we need world markets, more and more of them. Where are additional foreign markets to be found? It has been pointed out by leading economists and statesmen that more than a billion people throughout the world are potential consumers of our surplus products and that they could, under the right kind of governmental policies-including of course a liberal trade policy-be converted into actual consumers. All the great problems now facing the countiy-farm relief, agricultural surpluses, the utilization of manufacturing productivity, unemployment, maintenance of our standards of living, continued development and progress, international good will with resultant international peace- all seem to me to be bound up in the solution of this problem of the expansion of our foreign trade.

Unless the country is to abandon its high standards of living; unless our great manufacturing plants are to remain idle with accompanying unemployment; unless more and more farmers are to be driven from the land and forced to compete for a living with the surplus labour in the cities; unless progress and development are to cease and be followed by a recession, the result of which one can foretell, it seems to me we must abandon selfish and insular trade policies and set up a financial, commercial, economic policy that will be world-embracing in its aims. But the expansion of our foreign trade along the lines indicated can never be the policy of the Conservative party committed as it is to superprotection and economic isolation. It can come only by the ascendancy of the Liberal party with its broad and liberal tariff and trade policy that is a world policy. And that to my mind truly is the greatest of all Canadian policies-a Canada-first policy that means everything.
